messages.content: I want to develop semantic parsers that generalize to unseen operator compositions, even when training creates correlations between linguistic templates and program structure. What would that goal mean in concrete terms?

The aim is for a parser to recover the intended program structure rather than rely on a familiar linguistic template as a shortcut to that structure. The critical test concerns operator compositions not seen during training, under reversed template–structure correlations. The stated target is 80% exact-match accuracy on those held-out compositions. At the same time, the parser should retain in-distribution exact-match accuracy within two percentage points of an identically sized, conventionally trained parser.
Why specify the reversed correlations rather than simply say the compositions are unseen?

The two conditions test different aspects of generalization. Holding out operator compositions asks whether the parser can handle combinations beyond those encountered in training. Reversing the template–structure correlations makes the training association between a linguistic form and a program structure unreliable in the held-out setting. Together, they express the goal more precisely than “unseen compositions” alone.
So a parser could appear to handle new compositions while still leaning on the training correlation?

That is the concern the goal is designed to address. Success on an unseen composition would be less informative if the surrounding linguistic template still pointed toward the same sort of structure it tended to accompany in training. The reversed-correlation condition asks whether the parser can produce the exact intended structure when that association no longer provides the same cue. It does not, by itself, tell us how a particular parser would behave; it defines the intended challenge.
What exactly is meant by “exact match” here?

Exact-match accuracy counts a prediction as correct when the predicted program matches the intended program exactly under the evaluation's matching criterion. It is stricter than giving partial credit for a program that has some correct operators or an approximately right structure. The goal names exact match as the measure for both the held-out-composition target and the in-distribution comparison; it does not specify further details of the matching criterion.
Does the 80% apply to all evaluation settings?

No. The 80% exact-match target is specifically for held-out operator compositions under reversed template–structure correlations. The in-distribution requirement is expressed differently: its exact-match accuracy should be within two percentage points of the identically sized, conventionally trained parser. Those are two distinct requirements, not a single 80% threshold applied everywhere.
Can you unpack the in-distribution comparison without assuming a particular baseline score?

Let the conventionally trained parser's in-distribution exact-match accuracy be B%. The requirement is that the new parser's in-distribution exact-match accuracy remain within two percentage points of B%. That states a permitted difference from the comparison parser without supplying either parser's score. “Percentage points” describes the difference between accuracy rates; it is not a relative percentage change.
And the comparison is specifically to a parser of identical size?

Yes. The named reference is an identically sized, conventionally trained parser. Both parts matter: the in-distribution accuracy comparison is to conventional training, and the parser used for that comparison is the same size. The goal does not provide further properties of that parser, so there is no need to assume a particular architecture or training procedure beyond what is stated.
Is the in-distribution condition just secondary to the held-out target?

It is a separate requirement of the same goal. Reaching 80% exact-match accuracy on the held-out operator compositions under reversed correlations would address the specified generalization target. Retaining in-distribution exact-match accuracy within two percentage points of the identically sized, conventionally trained parser addresses the other stated concern: that this performance should not come with a larger in-distribution accuracy difference than the goal permits. Neither requirement substitutes for the other.
Would it be accurate to say the parser needs to ignore linguistic templates?

That would overstate the goal. Linguistic templates are part of the input's linguistic form; the issue is treating a training-time correlation between those templates and program structure as though it reliably determines the answer. The desired behavior is accurate parsing of the intended composition when that correlation is reversed, not a blanket refusal to use information in the language.
What does “operator composition” contribute to the wording? Why not just say unseen programs?

“Operator composition” identifies the aspect on which generalization is sought: how operators are combined in a program. “Unseen programs” would be broader and could include differences that do not specifically test composition. The goal does not say that every component of a held-out composition must itself be unseen; its stated focus is the unseen composition under the reversed template–structure correlations.
So this is not a claim that the parser already meets either number?

Correct. It states a development goal and two performance requirements, not a reported result. It calls for 80% exact-match accuracy on the specified held-out compositions and in-distribution exact-match accuracy within two percentage points of the specified comparison parser. No achieved scores are given.
Could someone satisfy the in-distribution comparison while missing the intended generalization result?

Yes, as a matter of what the requirements measure. Being close to the conventionally trained parser on in-distribution exact match does not establish 80% exact match on held-out operator compositions under reversed template–structure correlations. Conversely, the held-out target alone does not establish the in-distribution comparison. The goal requires both.
I'm trying to phrase the challenge without implying that every linguistic template maps to one fixed structure. How should I put it?

You can say that training contains correlations between linguistic templates and program structure, and that the held-out operator compositions are evaluated under reversed template–structure correlations. “Correlation” is the important word: it does not assert a fixed one-to-one mapping. The aim is for the parser to generalize despite those training correlations, rather than to assume they always identify the right program structure.
Is the reversal itself the goal, or a condition under which the generalization goal is judged?

It is a condition on the held-out target. The broader goal is to develop semantic parsers that generalize to unseen operator compositions despite training correlations between linguistic templates and program structure. The more precise performance requirement asks for 80% exact-match accuracy on held-out operator compositions under reversed template–structure correlations.
What would be lost if I described the aim only as improving out-of-distribution performance?

That description would leave out what is distinctive here. It would not identify unseen operator compositions, the reversal of the training template–structure correlations, or the 80% exact-match target. It would also omit the in-distribution safeguard: exact-match accuracy within two percentage points of an identically sized, conventionally trained parser. “Out-of-distribution performance” can be a useful broad description, but it cannot replace those specific conditions.
I also don't want the comparison phrased as if the two-percentage-point allowance applied to the held-out score.

Then keep the measures in separate clauses. One clause can state the 80% exact-match target for held-out operator compositions under reversed template–structure correlations. The other can state that in-distribution exact-match accuracy must remain within two percentage points of the identically sized, conventionally trained parser. That makes clear which threshold belongs to which setting.
Does the goal prescribe a way of training the new semantic parser?

No method for training the new parser is specified. “Conventionally trained” identifies the comparison parser for the in-distribution requirement; it does not prescribe an alternative training method for the parser being developed. The node sets out the desired generalization behavior and the two accuracy conditions, leaving implementation open.
Give me a compact statement that still keeps the full target intact.

Develop semantic parsers that generalize to unseen operator compositions despite training correlations between linguistic templates and program structure: achieve 80% exact-match accuracy on held-out operator compositions under reversed template–structure correlations, while retaining in-distribution exact-match accuracy within two percentage points of an identically sized, conventionally trained parser.
And if I explain it more conversationally?

You could say: “We want the parser to handle new ways of composing operators even when familiar linguistic templates no longer correlate with program structure as they did in training. The target is 80% exact match in that held-out, reversed-correlation setting, without moving more than two percentage points away from the in-distribution exact-match accuracy of a conventionally trained parser of the same size.”
Would “without losing more than two percentage points” be equivalent to “within two percentage points”?

“Without losing more than two percentage points” emphasizes avoiding a decrease, whereas “within two percentage points” states a difference from the comparison accuracy. To preserve the wording of the requirement most closely, use “within two percentage points.” In either case, the reference remains the in-distribution exact-match accuracy of the identically sized, conventionally trained parser, not the 80% held-out target.
One last distinction: is this a claim about a particular correlation causing errors, or about performance despite that correlation?

It is a goal about performance despite training correlations between linguistic templates and program structure. The reversed-correlation held-out condition makes dependence on those correlations a relevant concern, but the statement does not report an error analysis or establish a cause for any parser's mistakes. It specifies what a parser should achieve under that condition and how closely its in-distribution exact-match accuracy should track the stated comparison parser.
How could we turn that goal into a training proposal?

One proposal is to train a size-matched semantic parser using template-balanced utterance–program subtree recombinations and a span-to-operator contrastive loss, while retaining the original training examples. It is a proposed approach to the generalization goal, not a claim that the accuracy targets have been met.
Can you separate the parts of that proposal for me?

There is a size constraint on the parser, a way of constructing additional training material through utterance–program subtree recombinations, a balancing condition concerning linguistic templates, and a span-to-operator contrastive loss. The original examples stay in training alongside the recombinations. Each part belongs to the proposed training setup; the statement does not give a particular architecture, loss weight, or number of recombined examples.
What does “utterance–program subtree recombinations” mean at a high level?

It means recombining material on both sides of an utterance–program pair: linguistic material in an utterance and the corresponding subtree in its program representation. The paired aspect matters because the utterance and program should continue to express the same intended structure. The proposal names this kind of recombination but does not specify a particular algorithm for finding spans, choosing subtrees, or assembling the resulting examples.
Why include the program subtree rather than changing only the utterance?

The training item for a semantic parser pairs language with a program. If a recombination changes what the utterance expresses, its program side must reflect the corresponding change for the pair to remain coherent. Describing the operation as an utterance–program subtree recombination makes that paired change explicit. It does not imply that every possible recombination would produce a suitable training example.
And what is being balanced in “template-balanced”?

The qualifier concerns linguistic templates in the recombined training material. In the context of this goal, balancing is meant to keep a template from being an overly dependable shortcut to a particular program structure. The proposal does not define a template inventory, a numerical balance criterion, or exact counts, so those details should not be read into the phrase.
Is it fair to say that the recombinations are intended to loosen the association between templates and program structures?

Yes, as the proposed rationale. Template-balanced recombinations are aimed at reducing reliance on the training-time template–structure correlations that make the generalization goal difficult. That is a motivation for trying the method, not evidence yet that it works or that any particular correlation has been eliminated.
What role does the contrastive loss play alongside the recombinations?

The proposed span-to-operator contrastive loss focuses training on the relationship between linguistic spans and program operators. At a general level, a contrastive objective encourages a relevant span–operator association to be distinguished from alternatives. This complements the recombinations conceptually: the recombinations vary paired utterance–program material, while the loss emphasizes the link between language and operators. The proposal does not specify how alternatives are selected or how the contrastive term is combined numerically with the parser's other training objectives.
Should I describe it as teaching the model a fixed dictionary from words to operators?

No. “Span-to-operator contrastive loss” identifies a training signal involving spans and operators, but it does not assert a fixed one-to-one dictionary. A span's interpretation can depend on context and program composition. The proposal is to encourage useful span–operator distinctions, not to declare that every wording has one invariant operator mapping.
Why retain the original examples if we're adding recombinations?

Retaining them is an explicit part of the proposal. The recombined pairs supplement rather than replace the original utterance–program examples. That fits the aim of pursuing generalization while still attending to in-distribution accuracy, although retaining originals alone does not guarantee the required in-distribution result.
Could I say the proposal trains solely on a balanced recombined dataset?

That would conflict with the proposal's explicit instruction to retain original examples. You can say that training includes template-balanced utterance–program subtree recombinations and keeps the original examples. The statement does not fix their relative amounts or the order in which they are used.
How precise should I be about the size matching?

State that the proposed parser is size-matched. In light of the goal's in-distribution comparison, that means matching the size of the conventionally trained parser used as the comparison. It would go beyond the proposal to name a particular parameter count or architecture.
Does size matching itself make the comparison conclusive?

It controls the stated size comparison, but it does not establish either performance requirement. The proposal still needs to be assessed for exact-match accuracy on held-out operator compositions under reversed template–structure correlations and for in-distribution exact-match accuracy relative to the identically sized, conventionally trained parser. No results are supplied here.
Would both the recombinations and the contrastive loss be part of the same proposed training approach?

Yes. The proposal combines template-balanced utterance–program subtree recombinations with span-to-operator contrastive loss when training the size-matched parser, and it retains original examples. Presenting only one of those elements would leave out part of the stated proposal.
What should I avoid promising about the recombined examples?

Avoid claiming that every generated pair is valid, that a particular number is generated, or that recombination necessarily removes all template–structure correlations. The proposal names a template-balanced form of paired recombination; it does not provide construction rules, validation results, or a demonstrated effect. You can explain its intended role without reporting outcomes it has not supplied.
What should I avoid promising about the contrastive loss?

Do not specify an unstated formula, negative-sampling method, weight, or proven improvement. It is enough to say that a span-to-operator contrastive loss is included to encourage distinctions between linguistic spans and operators. How that signal is implemented and how much it helps are not specified.
Can you put the motivation and the proposal together without implying the experiment has already happened?

We could propose training a size-matched semantic parser on the original utterance–program examples plus template-balanced utterance–program subtree recombinations, with a span-to-operator contrastive loss. The intended rationale is to make the parser less dependent on training-time associations between linguistic templates and program structure while emphasizing how language relates to operators. Whether it meets the held-out and in-distribution exact-match requirements remains to be determined.
Is “template-balanced” describing the contrastive loss too?

As written, it describes the utterance–program subtree recombinations. The contrastive loss is separately described as span-to-operator. The two components are proposed together, but the wording does not say that the contrastive loss itself uses a template-balancing procedure.
If I say the method guarantees compositional generalization, is that too strong?

Yes. The proposal is intended to support generalization to unseen operator compositions despite template–structure correlations, but it does not guarantee that outcome. The goal sets a specific held-out accuracy target and an in-distribution comparison; the proposal supplies a training approach to consider, not evidence that those requirements are satisfied.
Can I describe the recombinations as paired changes rather than giving a concrete example?

That is a faithful way to keep the description general. You can say they recombine utterance material together with corresponding program subtrees, with balancing across linguistic templates. A concrete example would require choices about utterances, operators, and valid substitutions that the proposal does not supply.
How would you summarize the distinction between the two training components in one sentence?

The template-balanced utterance–program subtree recombinations vary the paired training examples, while the span-to-operator contrastive loss supplies an additional training signal about relationships between linguistic spans and program operators.
And the original examples are still there throughout this description?
Yes. Retaining original examples is not optional in the stated proposal. The precise way they are mixed with the recombinations is unspecified, but the proposal is not to discard them.
Let me check my wording: “Train an equally sized parser using balanced examples and contrastive learning.” Is that complete enough?

It captures the rough direction but loses important specifics. Say “size-matched parser,” identify the examples as template-balanced utterance–program subtree recombinations, identify the objective as span-to-operator contrastive loss, and explicitly say that original examples are retained. Otherwise the proposal could be mistaken for many different training approaches.
Please give me a concise version that preserves all of that.
Train a size-matched semantic parser with template-balanced utterance–program subtree recombinations and a span-to-operator contrastive loss, retaining the original examples.
Can template-balanced subtree swaps preserve quantifier and negation scope when their utterance spans overlap?

That is an open question for the proposed recombinations. A program subtree has a structural boundary, but its meaning may be expressed by an utterance span that overlaps language associated with another subtree. If a swap treats the spans as independent when they are not, the resulting utterance and program might disagree about what a quantifier or negation takes scope over. Template balance alone does not settle whether scope is preserved.
What makes scope different from simply keeping the same operators in the resulting program?

Scope concerns which part of an expression an operator governs, not just whether the operator appears. A program can still contain both a quantifier and a negation while placing one inside rather than outside the other. The utterance must support the same relationship. So preserving scope requires more than retaining the operator names on both sides of a recombined pair.
Is the overlap itself enough to show that a swap would be wrong?

No. Overlap is a reason to be careful, not proof that every swap changes meaning. It can indicate that the linguistic material relevant to one operator cannot be cleanly separated from the material relevant to another. Whether a particular recombination preserves scope depends on the resulting utterance and its paired program; the question does not establish an answer for all overlapping spans.
Could you clarify what ‘preserve’ means in this question?

It means preserving agreement between the utterance's scope interpretation and the scope encoded in the paired program after a swap. If the utterance expresses negation over a quantified expression, for instance, the program must express that same relationship; if the utterance expresses a different scope relationship, the program must reflect that instead. The issue is semantic agreement, not merely keeping the original ordering of words or operators.
Why might an utterance span associated with one subtree overlap another span?

An operator's interpretation can depend on language that also contributes to another operator's interpretation. Quantification and negation are especially relevant because their scope relationships concern larger expressions. An overlap can therefore make it unclear whether swapping what looks like one local piece of the utterance also changes the interpretation of material outside that piece. That is the concern the question raises, without assuming any particular span assignment has been made.
Does ‘template-balanced’ offer any protection against this problem?

Not by itself. Template balancing describes a property sought across the recombinations with respect to linguistic templates. Scope preservation concerns whether an individual recombined utterance and program encode compatible relationships between operators. A collection could be balanced across templates yet include pairs with incorrect scope, so the two issues have to be kept distinct.
Could I say that a valid subtree swap has to preserve the scope in the original program?

That wording may be too restrictive. A recombination could change the intended program, including a scope relationship, provided the resulting utterance and the resulting program agree. If the intended purpose of a particular swap is to keep a scope relationship unchanged, then it must preserve that relationship on both sides. The general requirement is that the new pair be semantically coherent, not that every detail always match the original pair.
So there are two possible errors: changing scope accidentally, or changing it in the program without matching the utterance?

Those capture the central concern. A swap might produce an utterance whose scope changes unintentionally while its program is left with the previous interpretation. Or the program might encode a new scope relationship that the utterance does not express. Either way, the utterance–program pair ceases to provide an unambiguous, matching training signal for that scope relationship.
Would retaining the original examples help answer whether the swapped ones preserve scope?

No. Retaining original examples is part of the training proposal, but it does not establish that a recombined example is scope-correct. The question is specifically about the validity of template-balanced subtree swaps when spans overlap. Keeping the originals does not resolve the meaning of a particular new utterance–program pair.
And the span-to-operator contrastive loss doesn't automatically resolve it either?

Correct. The proposed loss concerns relationships between linguistic spans and operators. It does not, just by being included, guarantee that an overlapping-span recombination preserves the relative scope of quantification and negation. The question is about whether the paired recombinations remain semantically sound under that overlap.
I want to be precise: are we talking about overlap between two program subtrees or between their utterance spans?

The question specifies overlap between their utterance spans. The program has its own structure, including the placement of quantifier and negation operators. The difficulty is that boundaries in the utterance may not separate as neatly as the program subtrees one might want to swap. It would be a different, broader question to ask about every form of overlap in program structure.
Suppose the spans are nested rather than merely sharing some words. Is that still within the question?

Yes, if ‘overlap’ is used broadly enough to include one span contained in another. Nesting can make the same issue especially clear: material associated with an outer scope relationship may include material associated with an inner one. But the question does not limit overlap to nesting or specify how spans are defined, so it should not be answered as though only that case matters.
Does the question assume that every overlapping span makes a clean subtree swap impossible?

No. It asks whether such swaps can preserve quantifier and negation scope; it does not assert impossibility. A conditional answer is more faithful: preservation is possible only where the resulting utterance's interpretation and the resulting program's scope agree, and overlap makes that agreement less safe to assume. The proposal as stated does not establish how often that condition can be met.
What is the risk of calling the utterance side a subtree too?

It could imply that the utterance comes with the same explicit tree boundaries as the program. The proposal calls for utterance–program subtree recombinations, but the question specifically concerns utterance spans that overlap. Keeping ‘utterance spans’ and ‘program subtrees’ distinct makes the issue clearer: a well-defined program subtree need not have an independent, nonoverlapping stretch of utterance that can be exchanged without affecting scope.
Could a sentence remain grammatical even if its paired program has the wrong quantifier or negation scope?

Yes, in principle. Grammaticality of the resulting utterance would not by itself show that its interpretation matches the program. The specific concern here is semantic scope: which expression the quantifier or negation governs. A plausible-sounding utterance could still express a different scope relationship from the one encoded by its paired program.
Then saying a swap ‘looks natural’ wouldn't answer the question.

Right. Naturalness and scope agreement are different considerations. To answer this question, one would need to know whether the recombined utterance expresses the quantifier and negation relationships represented by its program. The stated proposal does not supply enough detail or evidence to conclude that overlapping-span swaps satisfy that condition.
Does the word ‘can’ mean we only need to find some possible scope-preserving swaps?

It can be read as asking about possibility, but there is also a practical concern about the proposed class of recombinations. Showing that some overlapping-span swaps could preserve scope would not show that every such swap does, or that the proposal as a whole avoids scope errors. It helps to distinguish ‘possible in some cases’ from ‘reliably preserved by the proposed swaps.’ Neither conclusion is established in the question.
Would the concern still exist if a swapped program contained the correct quantifier and the correct negation?

Yes. The concern is their relative scope and what each governs. Correct operator identities alone do not ensure that the composed program means the same thing as the recombined utterance. In particular, the two operators can both be present while their scope relationship differs.
How can I state this as a focused objection without declaring the proposal unsound?

You could ask: ‘When utterance spans associated with quantifier and negation subtrees overlap, can the proposed template-balanced subtree swaps maintain agreement between the utterance's scope interpretation and the program's operator structure?’ That frames a specific validity question. It neither assumes that the swaps fail nor claims that they have already been shown to work.
Would that question be about the held-out accuracy target, or about the training pairs themselves?

Immediately, it is about the training pairs produced by the proposed recombinations: whether the utterance and program remain aligned in scope. It is relevant to the broader generalization goal, but it does not report or predict an exact-match accuracy figure. The 80% held-out target and the in-distribution comparison remain performance requirements, not answers to this scope question.
I should avoid saying the overlap necessarily reverses the scopes, then?

Yes. Overlapping spans do not necessarily reverse quantifier and negation scope. They raise the possibility that a swap changes or obscures the scope relationship, or that the program and utterance no longer agree. The question is whether preservation is achievable under those conditions, not an assertion that the reverse interpretation must result.
If the resulting utterance allows more than one scope reading, could I simply call the swap scope-preserving because one reading matches the program?

That would be a stronger conclusion than the question supports. A matching possible reading is not the same as establishing that the recombined example clearly expresses the program's scope. Ambiguity matters when asking whether the pair provides a reliable training signal. The question does not specify a policy for ambiguous utterances, so it is better to leave that issue open than to count such pairs as definitively scope-preserving.
So what's the shortest careful answer to my original question?

Possibly in some cases, but not automatically. When utterance spans overlap, template-balanced subtree swaps can preserve quantifier and negation scope only if the recombined utterance and its paired program still agree on what each operator governs. The proposal does not establish that this holds for overlapping spans.
Could we formulate a hypothesis that addresses the overlapping-span scope question?

Yes: scope-typed subtree swaps will maintain utterance–program scope agreement for at least 95% of overlapping negation–quantifier examples. That directly addresses whether swaps can preserve the relevant scope relationship when the utterance spans overlap. It is a hypothesis, not a measured result.
What does “scope-typed” contribute to that statement?

It qualifies the proposed subtree swaps: the hypothesis is about swaps that take scope into account through typing, rather than subtree swaps without that qualification. The statement does not define a type system or specify how a swap would be accepted or rejected, so we should not treat any particular implementation as part of the hypothesis.
Is the claim that 95% of swaps will be grammatical?

No. The predicted outcome is utterance–program scope agreement. An utterance being grammatical would not establish that it expresses the same negation–quantifier scope as its paired program. The threshold is at least 95% of the overlapping negation–quantifier examples, judged on that scope-agreement property.
Could you unpack “utterance–program scope agreement” again in this narrower setting?

For each relevant example, the scope relationship expressed by the utterance should match the scope relationship encoded by its program. With negation and a quantifier, the important question is what each operator takes scope over and how they relate to one another. The hypothesis predicts that scope-typed swaps maintain that agreement in at least 95% of examples where the associated utterance spans overlap.
Does “maintain” require the scope relationship to stay exactly as it was before the swap?

Not necessarily. The key relationship to maintain is agreement between the resulting utterance and its resulting program. If a swap changes the scope expressed by the utterance and the program changes correspondingly, the pair could still agree. The hypothesis does not say that every resulting pair must retain the original example's particular scope reading.
Why identify overlapping negation–quantifier examples specifically?

That is the class on which the hypothesis makes its quantitative prediction. It targets the scope concern raised when utterance spans associated with negation and quantification overlap. The statement does not extend the 95% figure to nonoverlapping spans, other operator combinations, or all recombined examples.
Would it be accurate to say the hypothesis promises perfect preservation in the difficult cases?

No. “At least 95%” is a threshold below 100%, and it is expressed as a prediction rather than a promise. It leaves open the possibility that some overlapping negation–quantifier examples will not have scope agreement after the swaps. It also leaves open whether the predicted threshold will be observed at all.
How should I read “at least 95%” mathematically?

It means 95% or more of the overlapping negation–quantifier examples in the relevant assessment would have utterance–program scope agreement after scope-typed subtree swaps. The hypothesis does not state how many such examples there are or provide an observed percentage.
If I call that 95% exact-match accuracy, would I be mixing up measures?

Yes. Here 95% concerns whether the utterance and program agree on scope in overlapping negation–quantifier examples. Exact-match accuracy, as used in the broader goal, concerns whether a parser's predicted program exactly matches its intended program. A scope-consistent recombined example is not itself a parser prediction, so the two percentages should not be conflated.
And the 95% isn't the target for held-out operator compositions?

Correct. The hypothesis's at-least-95% figure applies to utterance–program scope agreement for overlapping negation–quantifier examples produced by scope-typed swaps. It is distinct from the 80% exact-match target on held-out operator compositions under reversed template–structure correlations.
Could the scope hypothesis be true while the parser still fails to generalize?

Conceptually, yes. Scope agreement in recombined examples concerns the quality of those utterance–program pairs on one specified property. It would not by itself show that a trained parser reaches the held-out exact-match target or stays within the in-distribution comparison. The hypothesis addresses the scope question, not the entire performance goal.
Conversely, would good parser accuracy prove this particular hypothesis?

Not on its own. Parser accuracy and scope agreement in overlapping negation–quantifier training examples are different observations. To evaluate this hypothesis, the relevant question is whether the scope-typed swaps maintain agreement for at least 95% of that specified class of examples. A parser score alone would not supply that percentage.
Does the hypothesis say how overlap is identified?

No. It refers to examples in which the negation- and quantifier-related utterance spans overlap, but it does not define a span-identification procedure or an overlap criterion. Those details would matter to an eventual assessment, but they are not specified in the hypothesis.
Does it say what counts as a scope-typed swap?

It names scope-typed subtree swaps but does not give their construction rules. We can explain the intended distinction—scope is represented in the qualification on the swaps—without asserting a particular inventory of scope types, a swapping constraint, or a validation procedure.
Could I say scope typing prevents all scope errors before they occur?

That would go beyond the claim. The hypothesis predicts scope agreement for at least 95% of the specified examples, not that scope typing rules out every error. Nor does it establish a mechanism by which any remaining disagreements would arise.
What if an example includes both negation and quantification but their associated spans do not overlap?

It would not fall within the overlapping negation–quantifier class named in this hypothesis. The statement makes no quantitative prediction for nonoverlapping cases, even if they contain the same kinds of operators.
Does the wording limit us to a particular direction of negation–quantifier scope?

No. The stated criterion is agreement between the utterance and program about scope; it does not require one fixed ordering of negation and quantification across all examples. What matters is that each resulting pair expresses the same scope relationship on both sides.
Suppose someone asks whether template balancing is what delivers the 95%. What can we say?

The prediction is specifically about scope-typed subtree swaps. The broader proposal also discusses template-balanced recombinations, but this hypothesis does not isolate a causal contribution from template balancing or claim that balancing alone maintains scope. We should not attribute the predicted percentage to a component the hypothesis does not identify as its cause.
Does the scope-typed qualifier replace the earlier concern about overlapping spans?

It addresses that concern with a testable prediction rather than making the concern disappear. Overlap is still part of the condition: the hypothesis says the scope-typed swaps will maintain utterance–program scope agreement for at least 95% of overlapping negation–quantifier examples. Until assessed, it remains a prediction about those cases.
Would “scope-safe swaps” be an acceptable shorthand?

It risks implying that safety is already established or guaranteed. “Scope-typed subtree swaps” preserves the proposed intervention without building its hoped-for outcome into the name. You can then state separately the hypothesis that they will maintain scope agreement at the specified rate.
I also want to avoid making it sound as though 95% is an observed audit result.

Use predictive language: “We hypothesize that scope-typed subtree swaps will maintain utterance–program scope agreement for at least 95% of overlapping negation–quantifier examples.” That wording retains the threshold and population while making clear that the figure has not been reported as an observed result.
What is the narrowest question this hypothesis would answer if it were evaluated?

Whether scope-typed subtree swaps maintain agreement between the utterance's and program's negation–quantifier scope in at least 95% of examples with overlapping relevant utterance spans. That is narrower than asking whether all subtree swaps are valid, whether template correlations are resolved, or whether the trained parser meets its accuracy requirements.
Can you state the hypothesis once more, without adding an implementation or an outcome?
Scope-typed subtree swaps will maintain utterance–program scope agreement for at least 95% of overlapping negation–quantifier examples.
What would a concrete plan look like for examining whether swaps preserve scope when negation and quantifier spans overlap?

Annotate operator scopes, restrict swaps to compatible spans, and audit 200 overlapping negation–quantifier recombinations for scope agreement.
